title: Hitting, Biting, Kicking Isn't Misbehavior — It's a Preschooler Reclaiming Bodily Autonomy
dek: Stop asking how to make the hitting stop. For a three- or four-year-old, hitting, biting and kicking are often the only tool left to shout "I have no say" after adults have taken control of nearly everything their body does — give some choice back, and the behavior shrinks.
why: Most approaches restate "no hitting" and add punishment, never touching the need that precedes the behavior. This episode treats aggression as a need signal, and shows the scripts and cases for negotiating with teachers.
who: Parents whose child just started preschool and who keep getting calls home about incidents; and early-childhood teachers who want less aggression in the classroom without leaning on punishment.
skip: After 16:57 it's a course pitch; skip it if you only want the method itself.

points.h: Hitting is a child shouting that his body isn't his to run
points.body: Preschool is often the first place a child is controlled in nearly every bodily arrangement by an adult other than a parent: where to sit, how to sit, when to speak and when to move. For the previous three years he could roughly decide when to run and when to use the toilet. Sitting on a rug for 20 minutes without moving is a real deprivation of autonomy; and a three- or four-year-old has no language to assert "my body, my call," so hitting and kicking become one of the few tools still available. So when the call home comes, don't rush to lecture "hands to yourself" — ask instead: how much say did this child have over his own life before this, and what bit of it can be handed back now.

points.h: Kindergarten readiness is really obedience training
points.body: Teachers often say a given preschool has a high share of kindergarten-ready kids, and the core definition of that readiness is compliance: sit when the teacher says sit, even mid-task, even when the body is already overloaded. Parents fear that if the child doesn't comply now, he won't get into a good elementary school, college, a good life. But the price the child pays for that definition is learning to suppress the feeling of "what I need right now." Teachers aren't villains either — they too need to feel competent, need the kids safe, need to save effort, and may even get satisfaction from the power; many went into education precisely to repair their own childhood wounds, yet only know the power-over kind of relationship. Seeing both sides is what opens room to negotiate.

points.h: We grant ourselves regulation and deny it to children
points.body: If an adult at a party feels overloaded, she arrives early, leaves early, hides in a quiet room, even puts in noise-cancelling earplugs — we find that entirely natural. Turn the camera on a child, though, and apart from conventions like extra exam time, we immediately worry that "too much accommodation will spoil him, he'll never survive the real world." The truth is that adults grant themselves far more accommodation than they allow children. The source offers a concrete image: an adult stronger than you unceremoniously carries you out of the quiet room back into the middle of the loud party — as an adult you'd instantly see that as a violation of bodily autonomy; when it happens to a child we look right past it.

points.h: The repair point is before the behavior, not the behavior itself
points.body: Repeating "hitting is not okay" does nothing, because that isn't knowledge the child is missing. You need a different set of questions: what happened in the seconds before this bite? What happened earlier in the day? Is there a move or a new baby in the child's life? A sensory-overloaded child who gets jostled in line will melt down, so let him stand at the front, the back, or outside the line; a child who struggles with transitions needs a few minutes' warning. The adult analogy: when your partner snaps at you for no reason at night, it's usually not about that sentence but about the morning argument, the lack of sleep, a pile-up of stress. If the other person then tossed off "your attitude needs work," you'd blow up too — yet that's often the only version we give children.

points.h: Talking to the teacher: don't assign blame, hear what the "no" protects
points.body: Telling a teacher "please change what you do" almost always hits a wall. A safer opening is to drop judgment and reconstruct the facts: not who's responsible, just what actually happened; and include family changes, the context the teacher can't see. Once you know whether the trigger is sensory or autonomy, extend empathy to the three things behind the teacher: competence, the children's safety, and the relief of catching a breath. The request has to land on a concrete, doable change, like "could he sit on a ball outside the circle." If the teacher refuses, the key word isn't refusal — it's what need that "no" is still protecting, and finding a version that meets both sides.

points.h: One nap-time conflict, cleanly taken apart
points.body: When Jen's daughter Carys was three she couldn't nap, and the teacher wanted her lying down; she was bored and frustrated — her need was to play. The teacher had two needs: state rules required offering nap time, and nap time was the teacher's own break. The solution they found was to move her mat to a slightly separated corner, where she could quietly play with soft toys that wouldn't roll, and the teacher could see her through the window from the break room. The child kept her right to free play, the teacher kept the rule and the rest, and Jen escaped the no-win cycle of complaint calls. This segment shows "negotiating by need" isn't empty talk: everyone gives a little, but everyone's core need holds.

points.h: Every method comes down to one question
points.body: Compress all of the above into a single line: stop asking "how do I make the hitting stop," and ask "what need is this behavior communicating?" Hitting, biting and kicking are only surface signals; the real message may be "I need sensory relief" or "I need some say over my own body." Once the need is named correctly, a path to meeting it can be designed — and it is almost always the adult who changes the environment, because changing how the adult shows up is far easier than changing the child.

terms.def: The basic need to have choices over one's own life and body, and to act on one's own will.
An early-childhood metric for whether a child can sit still, follow instructions and adapt to group rules.
A change to the environment, rules or arrangements made to fit an individual's sensory needs or other needs.
An interaction model in which the adult holds the superior position and treats the child with commands and domination, as opposed to a collaborative model.

quotes.text: hitting or kicking can be one of the only tools that a three or four-year-old has for saying I don't have any say over what happens to my body right now and I need some of that.
When we imagine it happening to an adult we can kind of see it's an obvious violation of that person's body autonomy. And it is for a child too, it's just that we don't see it that way.
Being kindergarten ready means the child has learned that they are to do what an adult says even if that goes against what they know is right for their body.

But when we think about accommodations for kids unless it's for something like more time when they're taking a test we worry that they won't be able to survive in the real world if we accommodate them too much.
We know that we want that for ourselves, but somehow when kids are involved, we only focus on the behavior that we don't want to see and how do we change that?
And if the teacher says no, which they may do, what you're really listening for is what need they're trying to meet that underlies that no.
What need is this behavior communicating? Because from there you can find strategies to meet everyone's needs.
